sources.population: HandOA, explicitly distinguishing firstCMC and interphalangeal patterns
sources.outcomes: Consider exercise for pain/strength/function/mobility; CMC stability differs from IP exercise; thumb orthoses no proven deformity correction.
sources.uncertainty: Indexed recommendation passages inspected,not complete article inspection. No optimal exercise type/dose.
sources.limitations: Hand OA guidance supports education, ergonomic principles, activity pacing and assistive devices; consider exercise for pain, strength/function and mobility. Specifically notes first-CMC exercise differs from interphalangeal exercise. Thumb-base stability is relevant to thumb-base OA; do not relabel thumb-specific stability as an IP intervention. Thumb orthoses may reduce symptoms with longer use (at least 3 months in evidence); no demonstrated prevention/correction of deformity. No universal loading limit or optimal exercise dose. General hand-OA studies often mix joint distributions, limiting phenotype-specific extrapolation. Postoperative rehabilitation and inflammatory/erosive flares need separate applicability decisions.

sources.design: Systematic review adding 65 randomized studies; search through December 31, 2023.
sources.population: Mixed hand-OA phenotypes; new nonpharmacological studies did not specifically recruit inflammatory OA.
sources.comparator: Hand exercise versus no exercise; varied combinations
sources.outcomes: Low-certainty small long-term pain benefit from exercise, SMD −0.34 (95% CI −0.58 to −0.09); function/grip estimates very uncertain.
sources.uncertainty: Indexed relevant sections/tables inspected; not whole-article inspection; phenotype-specific effects unresolved.
sources.harms: None of the new exercise studies reported adverse events; earlier reports were few and often mild. Missing reporting is not zero harm.
sources.limitations: Added 65 RCTs since prior review; exercise studies heterogeneous/multimodal, with 11 new exercise trials. Pooled hand exercise versus no exercise showed low-certainty small long-term pain benefit (SMD −0.34, 95% CI −0.58 to −0.09); other functional/grip estimates very uncertain. No new exercise study reported adverse events; earlier reports had few, usually mild events. Missing reporting is not zero harm. Phenotype/subtype evidence insufficient; none of the new nonpharmacologic studies specifically recruited inflammatory OA. Review supports investigation without assigning thumb-CMC results to finger IP or a universal safe intensity.

sources.design: Cochrane review of exercise trials in hand OA.
sources.population: Mixed hand-OA populations; no isolated IP or CMC efficacy subgroup established.
sources.comparator: Varied exercise programs versus no exercise or other care.
sources.coInterventions: Education and supervision varied between trials.
sources.outcomes: Low-quality evidence for small short-term benefits. Included-study tables describe program components; individual component efficacy cannot be isolated.
sources.followUp: Commonly 12–13 weeks of intervention, with variable later follow-up.
sources.uncertainty: Dose tables are secondary extraction; exact primary handout/figures were not inspected. No single optimal regimen.
sources.harms: Hennig had one sustained-pain withdrawal; Østerås reported finger and neck/shoulder symptoms. Ascertainment incomplete.
sources.limitations: Small short-term pain/function/stiffness benefits with low-quality evidence; regimens, dose and comparators varied. Hennig's study-table dose: three sessions/week, 10 repetitions weeks 1–2, 12 weeks 3–4, 15 weeks 5–13. Exercises included O-sign, small/large fist, rubber-ball squeeze, band thumb abduction/extension, finger stretch. This is a secondary methods extraction; does not isolate each component. One Hennig participant withdrew with sustained pain; Østerås trial reported possibly related events. Review could not establish joint-subtype response. Exact dosing should be kept linked to its trial rather than becoming a universal hand-OA default.

protocol.execution: Hennig/Østerås programs include O-sign, small/large fist, ball/tube squeeze, band thumb abduction/extension and finger stretch. Østerås adds three shoulder exercises. Exact range/handout unavailable.
protocol.dose: Hennig: 10 repetitions weeks 1–2, 12 weeks 3–4, 15 weeks 5–13. Østerås: 10 initially, 15 weeks 3–12; tube squeeze held ten seconds. Secondary extraction only.
protocol.frequency: Three times weekly in Hennig/Østerås; other included trials differ.
protocol.supervision: Hennig: initial instruction and up to eight phone calls. Østerås: four group sessions plus home work and telephone contact.
protocol.progression: Study-specific repetition progression; does not establish load or joint response algorithm.
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as a validated universal rule; pain/sustained symptoms occurred.

sources.population: Physician-confirmed mixed hand OA; 90% women, mean age 66.
sources.comparator: Twelve-week group/home exercise versus usual care.
sources.coInterventions: Four group sessions and telephone contacts; program includes three shoulder exercises.
sources.outcomes: At three months, FIHOA difference −0.5/30 (95% CI −1.6 to 0.6), PSFS +0.9/10 (0.1 to 1.7), no grip/dexterity advantage. No significant group differences at six months.
sources.uncertainty: Small short-term benefits; no isolated IP/CMC effects established. Coexisting shoulder conditions matter.
sources.harms: Three possible finger pain/inflammation/swelling events; five neck/shoulder pain reports related to shoulder exercises, one withdrawal.
sources.limitations: 130 physician-confirmed hand-OA participants (90% women, mean age 66), 12-week group/home exercise versus usual care. Three weekly sessions; 10 repetitions initially, 15 after week 2; mixed hand/shoulder exercises. At 3 months FIHOA difference −0.5/30 (CI −1.6 to 0.6), PSFS +0.9/10 (0.1–1.7), small pain/stiffness changes; no significant group differences at 6 months. No grip/dexterity advantage. Primary report: three possible finger pain/inflammation/swelling events; five increased neck/shoulder pain reports related to shoulder exercises, one withdrawal. Shows limited durability and the need to respect other affected regions. Mixed hand OA does not provide isolated DIP/PIP effect sizes.

protocol.execution: Mixed program: O-sign, small/large fist, rubber-tube squeeze, band thumb abduction/extension, finger stretch, plus three shoulder exercises. See source Table 1; exact illustrated form requires review.
protocol.dose: Ten repetitions initially, fifteen after week two; rubber-tube isometric squeeze held ten seconds.
protocol.frequency: Three sessions weekly for twelve weeks.
protocol.supervision: Four group sessions plus home work and telephone contact.
protocol.progression: Ten to fifteen repetitions; moderate-to-vigorous intensity instruction was study-specific, not app clearance.
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as a validated universal numeric stopping threshold.

sources.design: Multicenter randomized trial; 166 adults at 18 Dutch clinics.
sources.population: Primary first-CMC OA, Eaton stage ≥2; comorbidity and prior-treatment exclusions constrain generalizability.
sources.comparator: Orthosis plus exercise, 81 patients, versus orthosis alone, 85.
sources.coInterventions: Custom orthosis in both groups; therapist education.
sources.outcomes: No significant three-month MHQ pain difference: +3.7/100 (95% CI −1.0 to 8.3). Surgery conversion 4.9% versus 9.4%, nonsignificant. Several secondary outcomes favored exercise.
sources.uncertainty: No primary-outcome superiority. Mean 7.4 actual therapy visits differs from 12 planned; this does not establish harmful alternative grip exercise.
sources.harms: Table 2 reports two grade-2 complications with exercise versus two grade-1 with orthosis alone, no grade-3 events. Event type and causal relation were not established here.
sources.limitations: No significant 3-month MHQ pain difference: +3.7/100 (95% CI −1.0 to 8.3); surgery conversion 4.9% versus 9.4%, nonsignificant. Some secondary outcomes favored exercise. [Registry](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05772715) planned 12 weekly 25–30-minute sessions plus home coordination, then strengthening; actual mean visits 7.4 (final PDF page 5). Table 2/page 9 reports two grade-2 complications with exercise versus two grade-1 with orthosis-only; no grade-3 events. Event type/causality not established here. Planned dose differs from adherence. No primary-outcome superiority or proof that other training is harmful.

protocol.execution: Thumb positioning/coordination followed by thenar strengthening alongside orthosis. Exact home-exercise sequence not independently verified from appendix.
protocol.dose: Three-month program; exact home repetitions and holds not established here.
protocol.frequency: Weekly therapy planned; actual mean 7.4 visits. Registry planned twelve 25–30-minute sessions, not observed adherence.
protocol.supervision: Trained hand therapists and home work across eighteen clinics.
protocol.progression: Registry: coordination initially six weeks, then strengthening and reduced orthosis use. Exact executions await appendix verification.
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as a validated exercise stopping rule.

sources.title: Effect of a stabilization exercise program versus standard treatment for thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis: A randomized trial
sources.publicationStatus: Final randomized trial, Journal of Hand Therapy 2023;36(3):546–559; online July 8, 2022.

access.details: Primary abstract and/or indexed source passages inspected; complete article inspection not established. Protocol fields deliberately not populated. [Primary abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35811182/). DOI 10.1016/j.jht.2022.03.009; PMID 35811182. 190 patients, mean 60, 78% women; standard care (orthoses, modalities, joint-protection education, adaptive equipment) with versus without stabilization home exercise over 6–12 months. Outcomes at 3/6/12 months; only 48% completed; groups could change after 6 months. No significant extra strength/ROM or patient-centered benefit from added exercise; poor/unknown adherence limits interpretation. Exact repetitions/holds unavailable in primary abstract. Harms not reported. Does not prove stabilization useless; supports uncertainty and avoidance of guaranteed benefit claims.
